The combustion test time was determined to be 1.0 s because the
pintle tip was damaged 0.7 s after normal combustion in the previous
combustion tests. When normal combustion occurs in the pintle injector,
the pressure fluctuations in the combustion chamber at the beginning of
combustion are attenuated and converges to a normal value..

However, as observed from the combustion test results presented in
Fig. 18, the combustion chamber pressure increased to 70 bara but the
initial pressure fluctuations were not damped. It is also observed that a
pressure drop occurs at 5.53 s (about 0.85 s after ignition) based on the
test sequence prior to closing the propellant supply valve from highfrequency pressure data shown in Fig. 19. This pressure change is
believed to be a phenomenon caused by the pintle tip thermal damage,
which is as shown in Fig. 20. The damage configuration of AI was
observed to be opposite to that of the insert nozzle wing position and
pintle tip side damage pattern. The fact that a part of the pintle tip re­
mains shows that the damage to the pintle injector AI began at the
rounded pintle tip. Thermal damage to the pintle tip occurred 0.2 s later
than that in A without the insert nozzle; moreover, the pintle tip is not
completely damaged, which is considered to be an effect of the insert
nozzle on cooling performance. The temperature of the pintle tip is also
lower than that of the model with the insert nozzle (AI) compared with
that without the insert nozzle (A), which is consistent with the results of
numerical analysis.

_5.2._ _Test results of BI-AM02_

Pintle injector BI has different _AR_, _BF_, and installed insert nozzle for
verification of the pintle tip cooling performance based on the _BF_ and
insert nozzle with the same number of orifices compared to the AI but
with lower _BF_ of 58% instead of 86% and _AR_ of 8:1 instead of 3:1. The
effects of the pintle tip cooling performance by the insert nozzle were
experimentally confirmed through the AI-AM02 combustion test. From
the results of numerical analysis, the pintle tip temperature of the pintle
injector BI with the insert nozzle was confirmed to be lowest, so a hot
firing test (5.0 s) was performed by combining BI and AM02. As shown
in Figs. 21 and 22, the combustion tests were completed normally
without any notable issues until the end of the burn, except for the lowfrequency fluctuations during the transient ignition period.

The low-frequency fluctuations at the beginning of combustion were
similar to those in the previous pintle tests of AI-AM02. It did not occur
in the turbo pump test facility, but only in the pressure-fed facility, are
considered to be the effects of the propellant supply method of the
pressure-fed test facility. The fast fourier transform for the dynamic
pressure of the combustion chamber corresponding to the transient re­
gion after ignition is shown in Fig. 23. The frequency analysis shows that
maximum fluctuations occur at 97.6 Hz, whose size is 0.14 bar in all
manifolds. The high-frequency pressure fluctuations of the combustion
chamber in the steady state operation cause maximum fluctuations
owing to the boiling of propellant in the low-frequency region of 146 Hz,
but the low-intensity pressure fluctuations were maintained overall. The
root mean-squared (RMS) value of the pressure fluctuations, as shown in
Fig. 24, are also maintained at the 0.5 bar level except for the initial
ignition, indicating that stable combustion was achieved.

The pintle injector after the combustion test is shown in Fig. 25. A
large amount of soot was formed near the head plate and pintle tip,
where a low-mixing-ratio region was formed in the pintle injector. The
soot around the pintle orifice was generated about 30% in the longitu­
dinal direction of the 1st pintle orifice and about 50% at the bottom of
the 2nd pintle orifice. It is considered that the flame is generated by
collision and mixing of the propellant in the primary orifice, and addi­
tional flames are generated at the bottom of the secondary pintle by the
high-temperature recirculation zone formed at the center of the pintle.
Comparing the shapes of the soot between the 1st and 2nd orifices of A,
AI, and BI (Fig. 26), a soot-free area is observed in BI (with _BF_ 57%), but
A and AI (with _BF_ 86%) have soot formation in all areas.

Therefore, some annular fuel flow from the wide rib between the 1st
and 2nd orifices of BI does not participate in combustion, which exits to
the 2nd orifice and participates in the combustion of the core recircu­
lation region with high mixing ratio (Fig. 4). Accordingly, the mixing
ratio is lower than those of pintle injectors A and AI and is believed to
contribute to the increase in the cooling effects of the pintle tip..

_5.3._ _Test results of BI-AM01~AM04_

A 20-s hot firing test was performed at the design point to verify the
effects of pintle tip cooling and combustion performance characteristics
based on the _TMR_ . Damage to the pintle tip did not occur in the hot firing
test with the combination of four annulus rings. The propellant flow rate
supplied to the combustor was controlled via pressure control in the
pressure-fed test facility, and the changes in the propellant flow rate
affected the _TMR_ and characteristic velocity efficiency. Therefore, to
compare the combustion characteristics under similar test conditions,
the combustion test data were averaged at 1-s intervals and then filtered.
Filtering was performed under the conditions of a mixing ratio 2.415 ±
0.035 and total mass flow rate of 4.46 ± 0.16, and the average of the
filtered values is presented in Table 6.

Changes in the combustion performance based on the total mo­
mentum ratio are shown in Fig. 27 with uncertainty [40–42]. From the
results of the analysis, the highest characteristic velocity efficiency of
94.83% was achieved in AM04 with a design momentum ratio of 0.78,
and it was confirmed that as the annulus orifice gap decreased, the TMR
increased and performance decreased. The relationship between the
TMR and characteristic velocity efficiency is similar to the results re­
ported in previous studies [13,19].

The changes in heat flux based on the _TMR_ and _O/ F_ ratio are shown
in Figs. 28 and 29 with uncertainty. The heat flux of the combustion
chamber tends to increase markedly as the mixing ratio increases, except
for AM02, and decreases as the TMR increases. The reason for this is that
the amount of propellant that collides with the combustion chamber
wall increases as the _TMR_ increases, which manifests as film cooling
effect. This means that the amount of propellant that does not partici­
pate in the combustion increases. Thus, it was found that the charac­
teristic velocity efficiency decreased. Therefore, it can be considered
that the cause of the low heat flux of AM02 is due to the mixing ratio.

For all models in Tables 4 and 5, the combustion pressures were
predicted to be around 60 bara, which was lower than the actual target
combustion pressure of 70 bara. This means that as noted in Ref. [43],
the currently used turbulence model standard K-ε model shows that the
combustion reaction is not achieved completely. Owing to the low res­
olution of the grid, the turbulent mixing efficiency was much lower than
the actual value, so it is estimated that the unburned propellant escaped
through the nozzle before the chemical reaction. However, it is possible
to quantitatively compare the changes in combustion pressure and
combustion characteristics based on the _TMR_ . From the analysis, it was
predicted that the combustion pressure and combustion efficiency
increased inversely with _TMR_, and the maximum combustion efficiency
was predicted for AM04, which is similar to the combustion test result.
Therefore, it is determined that the characteristic velocity efficiency also
increases with improvement in the relative mixing efficiency of fuel and

oxidizer via increase of the flow velocity of fuel by reducing the gap size
of the annulus ring.

**6.** **Conclusion**

A 1.5-tonf class liquid–liquid pintle injector with rectangular tworow orifices using kerosene/liquid oxygen as the propellant was
designed and manufactured, and hot firing tests of the pintle injector
were carried out to verify the combustion performance and combustion
stability under supercritical conditions, which is the actual operational
condition of the liquid rocket engine. Thermal damage occurred at the
pintle tip owing to the high mixing ratio recirculation region formed
within the combustion chamber. To increase the cooling effect, the
design of the pintle injector was changed by installing an insert nozzle.
Then, numerical analysis was performed on the pintle injector with
different design parameters to confirm the effects on pintle tip cooling
and changes in combustion performance. Finally, combustion tests were
performed and the following results were obtained.

1) In the numerical analysis results, it was observed that the insert
nozzle had an effect of up to 21.4% on pintle tip cooling, which was
confirmed through the combustion tests of pintle injectors A and AI.
2) From the numerical analysis results, it was considered that the
combustion pressure and combustion efficiency increased inversely
with the _TMR_ . Similar results were confirmed by performing com­
bustion tests on pintle injectors BI-AM01 to BI-AM04, and a
maximum characteristic velocity efficiency of 95.1% and combus­
tion pressure of 69.9 bara were achieved with BI-AM04 ( _TMR_ of
0.72).
3) The heat flux of the combustion chamber increased markedly with
the mixing ratio and decreased with increase in _TMR_ . Further, it was
found that the characteristic velocity efficiency decreased.
4) From the numerical analysis results, the pintle tip temperature was
observed to reduce by 9.5–21.4% depending on the presence or
absence of the insert nozzle. In addition, the effects of reducing the
pintle tip temperature by 17.3% were confirmed by changing the _BF_
from 86% to 58%, which means that the pintle tip temperature of the
pintle injector BI with the insert nozzle was the lowest.
5) When the AR is increased from 3:1 to 8:1 and _BF_ is reduced from 86%
to 58%, the injected fuel pushes the flames outward from the pintle
tip or forms a low-mixing-ratio region at the pintle tip; further, the
insert nozzle installed within the pintle has been identified as a major
factor affecting the thermal damage to the pintle tip. Finally, similar
results were confirmed from the numerical analyses and hot firing
tests for the pintle tip thermal damage. However, there is a limit to
designing a pintle injector with optimal performance only from the
results of this study, and studies on the parameters (BF, TMR and
orifice configuration) of liquid-liquid pintle injectors will be con­
ducted under critical combustion.
